Generation two goes to school. As adults they have unhappy memories of curriculum Y and change it for their children. But curriculum X has gone down the memory, so they revive aspects of X that didn't work for generation one.

So the main point of the dumbed down kiddy version is to talk about generational forgetting. There is usually a history behind what is on the curriculum. Sometimes that history justifies a lesson. Sometimes that history lets us say "times have changed" and discard a lesson with a clear conscience.

Example: Pencil and paper methods for arithmetic. Especially long division. The method I was taught as a child in 1970 was OK, but it had three underlying assumptions. First, children had drilled to fluency with multiplying a string of digits by single digit. Second, paper was expensive, the method had to be concise. Third, one is planning to drill for speed, not just understanding. So when it came to dividing 6789 by 1234 the child was supposed to find the first digit by mental arithmetic. It looks like 1234 goes into 6789 around 6 times. No, wait, six twelves is 72, that is too much. Must be five times.

So one writes 5, computes 5x1234 and puts 6170 under 6789 and subtracts getting 619. Bring down a zero and we are faced with dividing 6190 by 1234. And we are faced with the same farting about. How many times does 1234 go into 6190.

This sets up a story of pencil and paper methods versus calculators. Generation one resents being drilled in paper and pencil methods. As adults they use calculators. So pencil and paper methods get dropped.

Generation two notices that they keep getting into debt. They can do they sums on a calculator, but they lack emotional weight, and they still take out the loan. Pencil and paper methods go back into the curriculum.

But with a misplaced emphasis on drilling for speed and not wasting paper. So you can see trouble coming as Generation three resent their boring drill.

Punchline: if you are going to do a long division using pencil and paper, for example 6789 divided by 1234, start by writing out your 1234 times table for 1 to 9. 1 x 1234 = 1234; 2 x 1234 = 2468; 3 x 1234 = 3702; 4 x 1234 = 4936; 5 x 1234 = 6170; 6 x 1234 = 7404; 7 x 1234 8638; 8 x 9872; 9 x 1234 = 11106.

That wastes time and wastes paper; it is not authentically old-school. Also, it makes long division a lot easier. You can look at 5 x 1234 = 6170 and 6 x 1234 = 7404, both written down on the paper in front of you, and at 6789 and see 6170 < 6789 < 7404. We clearly start five and a bit, and must do more work to compute the bit. It is no longer a weed-out challenge.

But all that is fine. We are only studying paper and pencil methods to build the kind of understanding that gives emotional weight to the results of the calculation. We need to say no to that loan! But as adults, we will mostly be using calculators or computers.
